extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics; poets and teachers of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards used in Hazlitt's lectures for judging the qualities of major English poets (Chaucer, Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton) — e.g., imagination, character, language, versification, passion, genre‑suitability. Useful for literary criticism and assessing poetic greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination (power of feigning things according to nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: "imagination, that is, the power of feigning things according to nature" (Hazlitt's phrase describing a core faculty of great poets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is the fundamental ability to 'feign'—to invent or represent things—but always 'according to nature' so they seem believable. Hazlitt treats this as common to Chaucer, Spenser, Shakspeare, and Milton while noting that the moving power or emphasis of that imagination differs between them (habit, novelty, passion, morality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and individuality of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be "as much itself, and as absolutely independent of the rest, as well as of the author, as if they were living persons, not fictions of the mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great dramatic characters feel autonomous: they speak and act as if they existed independently of the poet. Hazlitt emphasizes that each character must have distinct physiognomy and inner life (examples: Caliban, Ophelia) and that dialogue should reveal that individuality rather than read like authorial exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and dramatic truth of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogues should appear to be "carried on without any consciousness of what is to follow, without any appearance of preparation or premeditation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue must feel unrehearsed and natural—utterances should seem to spring from character and situation, not from the author's rhetorical design. Hazlitt cites Shakespeare's dialogues as exemplars where lines emerge 'as if by touching a secret spring.' Anti-pattern: stilted or stagey speeches that reveal the author's hand rather than the character's spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion: dramatic fluctuation and modification
rubrics_metrics.description: "The passion in Shakspeare is... passion modified by passion...subject to all the fluctuations of caprice and accident; calling into play all the resources of the understanding and all the energies of the will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion should be dynamic, variable, and influenced by other feelings and circumstances (not a single obsessive mood). Hazlitt praises dramatic fluctuation—small causes can instantly provoke large effects (example: Iago's suggestions to Othello). Anti-pattern: flat, monolithic feeling that does not interact with situation or other motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety, range and universality of mind (generic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare's "generic quality, its power of communication with all other minds... it contained a universe of thought and feeling within itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great poet/ dramatist demonstrates intellectual and emotional range, able to represent many types of persons and situations empathetically. Hazlitt regards this universality as a key excellence of Shakespeare—he can 'be like all other men.' Caution: excessive variety without restraint can disperse effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and aptness of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: "In Shakspeare, any other word but the true one, is sure to be wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction must be precisely chosen: the 'true' word or epithet gives an image or feeling ineluctably. Hazlitt notes Shakespeare's epithets and phrases as 'like sparkles'—concise verbal hits that are hard to substitute. Anti-pattern: lazy or approximate diction where a precise phrase is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification and musical harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Versification should supply 'the most smooth and the most sounding' music—'a labyrinth of sweet sounds...linked sweetness long drawn out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter, stanza-form, cadence and sound-patterns must be adapted to the poet's aims: Spenser's stanza yields 'melting harmony' and 'linked sweetness', Shakespeare's blank verse is readably varied and alive. Hazlitt values rhythmic variety and relief from monotony; but he also judges forms by their fit with language (see Spenser stanza comments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form suitability and formal innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms must suit the language and purpose: Spenser's stanza is 'borrowed from the Italians' and not perfectly adapted to English, yet forced invention of new forms produced a rich poetic language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether stanzaic choice and formal devices are appropriate for the language and material. Innovation is valuable when it produces new expressive resources; faults may arise from forcing unsuitable foreign forms, but necessity can yield 'a poetical language rich and varied.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of strength (visionary/vast vs. active/willed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser's strength is not 'strength of will or action...nor is it coarse and palpable--but it assumes a character of vastness and sublimity seen through...visionary medium.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between kinds of poetic 'strength': visceral, dramatic force (action, will) versus visionary, sublime massiveness (romance, distant terror). Evaluate whether the poet's chosen strength fits the work's aims (e.g., Spenser's large, visionary force suits allegory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos: sentiment versus immediate action
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser 'has not indeed the pathos of immediate action or suffering, which is more properly the dramatic; but he has all the pathos of sentiment and romance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different poets achieve pathos differently: dramatic pathos (immediate action, suffering) or sentimental/romantic pathos (distance, meditated feeling). Critique should note which mode is in play and whether it succeeds for the material (examples: Cave of Despair, change of Malbecco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and verisimilitude of scene and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: When Shakespeare conceives a character 'he not only entered into all its thoughts and feelings, but seemed instantly...to be surrounded with all the same objects...the scenery and situation...are given with a miraculous truth of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters come with a coherent world—time, place, custom and incidental detail that make their speech and action believable. Hazlitt admires scenes where every object exists 'as it would have existed in reality.' Lacking this coherence, characters feel flat or stagey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic character development through action and contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare's characters are 'historical figures...put into action, where every nerve and muscle is displayed in the struggle with others, with all the effect of collision and contrast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer characters revealed and transformed by conflict and interaction rather than static portraits. Hazlitt contrasts Chaucer's steady physiognomical studies with Shakespeare's characters who change under pressure—criticism should ask whether the work uses interaction to deepen character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of metaphor and associative felicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare 'brings together images the most alike, but placed at the greatest distance from each other...Their felicity is equal to their force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet's facility for surprising, remote associations that cohere powerfully (e.g., Troilus and Cressida lines quoted). Such combinations should feel fresh and illuminating, not forced or incoherent. Mixed metaphors can be idiomatic in Shakespeare's hands but hazardous for lesser voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial richness and picturesque imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser's descriptions 'have high picturesque character' and 'Nobody but Rubens could have painted the fancy of Spenser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the vividness and painterly quality of imagery: does the poem create striking visual tableaux (examples: Cave of Mammon, Satyrane taming lion's whelps)? This criterion rewards richly pictured scenes and careful distribution of sensory detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral elevation and breadth of ideal view
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton is described as 'the poet of morality' whose imagination is 'nigh sphered in Heaven' and who raises principles 'to the utmost conceivable grandeur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a poet attains moral elevation or universality of idea appropriate to epic and high subject-matter. Hazlitt treats Milton's moral, elevated tone as a distinct excellence—judge whether the seriousness and elevation fit the work's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of narrow personal egotism; balance between imagination and sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'great fault of a modern school of poetry is, that it is an experiment to reduce poetry to a mere effusion of natural sensibility... to surround the meanest objects with the morbid feelings and devouring egotism of the writers' own minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt warns against poetry that is merely self-absorbed mood (morbid egotism) and that surrenders imaginary splendour and human passion for private feeling. Critique should test whether sentiment is universalized by imagination or collapses into personal solipsism.
